Decline the relationship, because former senior officials cannot open private banking accounts for a period after retirement
Treat only his family members as PEPs, not him
quiz.explanation: PEP declassification is risk-based, not automatic after a fixed period. A former senior official may retain influence and corruption risk. Declining outright is not required; enhanced measures can manage the risk.

quiz.question: A local welfare trust applies for an account. One of its trustees shares his full name with a person on the UN Security Council sanctions list. What should happen before the account is opened?
options: Check identifiers such as passport number, date of birth and nationality to resolve the match, and escalate to compliance
Open the account because the trust is registered and provides welfare services
Remove the trustee's name from the account documents and proceed
Ask the trustee directly whether he is the person on the list, record his answer and proceed if he denies it
quiz.explanation: A potential match must be resolved using identifiers such as passport number, date of birth and nationality and escalated to compliance; a true match means funds must not be made available. Registration does not cure the risk, removing the name hides a controller, and asking the trustee could warn him and proves nothing.

quiz.question: When a bank provides correspondent services to a foreign respondent bank, which of these is required?
options: Treating the respondent as low risk if it is in a FATF member country
Relying on the respondent's own AML/CFT compliance certificate and questionnaire, signed by its chief compliance officer
Assessing the respondent's business, controls and supervision, obtaining senior management approval, and excluding shell banks
Opening the account first and assessing the respondent within one year
quiz.explanation: Correspondent relationships require assessment of the respondent's business, supervision and AML/CFT controls, senior management approval, clear responsibilities and a shell bank prohibition. FATF membership does not make a bank low risk, and a self-certificate alone is not enough.

quiz.question: During account opening, Nimra develops a strong suspicion that the applicant is laundering fraud proceeds. Continuing to ask detailed CDD questions would likely alert him. What do the standards permit?
options: Opening the account to avoid suspicion, then filing an STR next year
Telling the applicant politely that compliance has concerns about him
Completing all CDD first, regardless of the tipping-off risk
Stopping the CDD process and escalating so that an STR can be filed
quiz.explanation: Where pursuing CDD would tip off the customer, institutions may stop the process and file an STR instead. Telling him about concerns is tipping off, and opening the account and delaying the report defeats both CDD and prompt reporting.

quiz.question: An inspector asks a branch to produce the CDD file for a customer whose account was closed six years ago. The country's law requires key records to be kept for ten years. The branch says it destroyed them after five years 'under the FATF minimum'. What is the issue?
options: The branch breached the local retention requirement; FATF's five years is a floor, not a ceiling
There is no issue, because FATF's minimum period has passed
There is no issue, because closed accounts are outside record-keeping rules
The only issue is that the branch should have scanned the records before destroying the paper files
quiz.explanation: FATF's five years is a minimum, and countries such as Pakistan require longer retention for key records; the local law applies. Closed accounts remain covered, and scanning is irrelevant if the records were destroyed before the required period ended.

sessions.title: Monitoring, Red Flags and Reporting to the FIU
sessions.summary: At the listening post you learn to hear what transactions are saying. Recognise red flags in branches, trade, remittances and digital channels, investigate alerts properly, escalate internally, and report to your FIU without tipping off the customer.
objectives: Explain how ongoing and transaction monitoring work and how alerts should be investigated and closed
Recognise red flags for branch cash activity, money mules, trade-based money laundering, remittances and digital channels
Decide when an STR is required and write a clear, useful STR narrative
Distinguish STRs from cash threshold reports and explain the reporting route to the FIU
Apply the tipping-off prohibition and the internal escalation process, learning from real monitoring failures

cards.title: The alert queue lights up
cards.setting: The Listening Post: the monitoring room, Kuala Lumpur, 8:45 am. Three screens, one teh tarik each.

lines.text: (on screen from Dubai) Overnight alerts. Victor Lau's account: 41 cash deposits in three weeks, all of similar size, just under the level that triggers extra counter checks, at seven branches.
And London: one app account opened last week received 37 small transfers from strangers in two days. Each was moved out within minutes.
It gets better. Yesterday Victor asked my teller, 'How much cash can I deposit without the bank reporting it?'
What did the teller say?
Nothing yet. She came straight to me. She's nervous about getting it wrong.
Good instinct. Today is about hearing what transactions are saying, and reporting it right without letting the customer know.

scenes.heading: Two kinds of ears
scenes.narration: Monitoring compares what a customer does with what CDD told us to expect. Systems run rules tuned to our risk assessment, and people notice what systems can't, like a depositor who doesn't know the account holder's name.

scenes.heading: Review and gather
scenes.narration: An analyst checks the alert against the profile and history, then gathers more: related accounts, counterparties, past alerts, open sources, and careful routine questions through the relationship manager.

scenes.heading: Decide
scenes.narration: Is there a reasonable explanation, or are there grounds to suspect? Many alerts close legitimately. Filing everything 'to be safe' is defensive filing, and it buries real intelligence.

scenes.heading: Write down why
scenes.narration: 'Customer is genuine, closed' is not a rationale. 'Matches the festive-season sales pattern of the last three years, with normal counterparties' is. Someone must be able to check your decision later.

scenes.heading: Backlogs are risk
scenes.narration: An alert reviewed three months late is a report filed three months late. Inspectors treat alert backlogs as a serious finding.

cards.title: Red flag or normal activity?
cards.prompt: Sort each pattern from this week's alerts. Red flags call for a closer look; normal activity can be closed with a rationale.

items.text: Repeated cash deposits just below a threshold, spread across branches
A garment retailer's cash deposits rise before the festive season, as in the last three years
A self-described cook receives remittances from 12 unrelated senders and withdraws cash the same day
Monthly salary credits from the same employer
A new wallet receives dozens of transfers from strangers and empties within minutes
One large cash deposit backed by a registered property sale deed
A branchless agent processes ten times the volume of nearby agents, for a few wallets
A 'freelancer' converts foreign currency daily with no documents and pays unrelated businesses
A customer asks how much he can deposit without the bank reporting it

cards.title: From millions of transactions to one STR
cards.caption: Each narrowing step needs judgement and a written rationale.

items.label: All transactions
items.detail: Every deposit, transfer, remittance and trade payment.

items.label: Alerts
items.detail: Rules and staff observations flag activity that doesn't fit the profile.

items.label: Investigated cases
items.detail: Analysts review, gather information and document a decision.

items.label: Internal escalations
items.detail: Cases with possible grounds for suspicion go to the compliance officer.

items.label: STR filed with the FIU
items.detail: Filed promptly once suspicion is formed.

cards.question: Kwame reviews an alert on a rice wholesaler whose cash deposits jump every harvest season, exactly as in the previous two years, with the usual suppliers. What is the right outcome?
options: File an STR anyway, to be safe
Close it with a note saying 'customer is genuine'
Close it with a rationale citing the seasonal pattern, prior years and normal counterparties
Ask the FIU whether the alert can be closed
cards.explanation: Activity that matches a documented pattern can be closed, but the rationale must show what was reviewed and why it fits. Filing without grounds is defensive filing, a one-line note can't be checked, and the FIU doesn't advise on individual alerts.

cards.title: Name that typology
cards.prompt: Match each typology to the pattern that gives it away.

pairs.right: Many deposits of similar amounts kept just under a threshold, across days or branches
A newly opened account collects transfers from many strangers and passes them on within minutes
Undocumented currency conversion, then payments to unrelated businesses for others
Goods shipped at prices far below market, so part of the value stays abroad and is settled informally
Paying a supplier far more than the goods are worth, often with lower values declared to customs
A branchless agent's volume dwarfs its peers, concentrated on a handful of wallets

cards.title: Real case: NatWest and the jeweller's cash
cards.body:
**What happened.** Fowler Oldfield, a jewellery business in Bradford, England, banked with NatWest. Its expected turnover at onboarding was modest, yet between 2012 and 2016 about **GBP 365m** was paid into its accounts, around **GBP 264m** of it in cash.

**The red flags, as set out in court:**
- cash deposited at branches around the country, at one point in bin bags
- volumes far above the customer's profile
- staff raised concerns, but a system error meant some cash was not treated as cash by monitoring, and alerts were not acted on effectively

**Outcome.** In 2021 NatWest pleaded guilty to three offences of failing to comply with the UK Money Laundering Regulations 2007, the first criminal prosecution of a bank under those rules, and was fined about **GBP 265m**.

**Lesson:** compare activity with the CDD profile, and act on what staff see at the counter.

cards.title: Fabric at 40 percent off
cards.setting: Trade operations, Singapore. Mei Lin Tan has asked for a video call.

lines.text: Riverbend Textiles, an eight-year customer of our Singapore desk. Their new buyer is a free-zone trading firm, and it pays 40 percent less per metre than their European buyers.
The buyer's address is a business centre hosting hundreds of companies. Part of the proceeds come from two unrelated firms in another country.
And one of those payers? Quillon Trading's sister company. The trail runs straight through your LCs, Mei.
The RM says it's 'clearance stock'. But the shipping documents say first-quality fabric.
Under-invoicing lets part of the true value stay abroad, settled informally. Mei, record the price comparison and escalate it through the trade AML checklist.
Now we have three strands that look suspicious. Time to learn how an STR actually gets made.

cards.title: Escalation to STR, step by step
cards.prompt: Put the path from a teller's concern to a filed STR in the right order.
steps: Notice the red flags and write down the facts you saw
Escalate promptly on the internal form to the designated AML contact
Compliance reviews the case and gathers further information
The compliance officer decides whether to file and documents the reasons either way
Compliance files the STR promptly with the FIU, often through its online system such as goAML
Keep monitoring, decide the relationship on risk, and tell no one who doesn't need to know

cards.title: STR versus CTR
cards.caption: Not every country uses cash threshold reports, and thresholds differ: the US uses USD 10,000 and Australia AUD 10,000. In the US, splitting cash to dodge the report is itself a crime. Check your local rules.
headers: STR (SAR in the US and UK)

items.label: Trigger
items.left: Suspicion or reason to suspect ML/TF
items.right: Cash at or above a set threshold, where the country uses such reports

items.label: Judgement
items.left: Yes: analysis and a documented decision

items.label: Replaces the other?
items.right: Never replaces an STR; suspicious large cash needs both

items.label: Why accuracy matters
items.left: Clear facts let FIU analysts act
items.right: Correct ID numbers let the FIU link cash with other intelligence

cards.title: 'How much can I deposit without a report?'
cards.situation: Victor Lau is back at Aisyah's counter with a bag of cash. He leans in and asks the teller again: 'Just tell me the amount I can deposit without the bank reporting it. Everyone knows there's a limit.' Two customers are waiting behind him. Aisyah is standing nearby. What should the teller do?

choices.text: Tell him the exact threshold. The rules are public anyway.
choices.outcome: The teller has just helped a customer plan structuring. That can amount to facilitating it, and the next week's deposits arrive neatly below the line.

choices.text: Say politely that the bank follows its standard procedures for all deposits, don't advise on reporting, then escalate his question internally.
choices.outcome: Victor grumbles but deposits nothing that day. The teller's internal note, with his exact words and time, becomes a key fact in Kwame's analysis. Professional, honest and no tip-off.

choices.text: Tell him every deposit is reported, so there's no point asking.
choices.outcome: Partly right: it avoids helping him structure, but it is untrue and unprofessional, and false statements can come back to haunt the bank. The teller also still needs to escalate his question internally.

choices.text: Refuse to serve him and announce that his account will be closed.
choices.outcome: Disproportionate and loud. A sudden, public closure signals suspicion and may tip off him and his associates while the case is still being built.

cards.front: Is there a minimum amount for an STR?
cards.back: No. Any amount can be reported, including tiny transfers that may be terrorist financing.

cards.front: The customer walked away when asked about the source. Report?
cards.back: Possibly. Attempted transactions count. Escalate if there are grounds for suspicion; don't phone him to ask why he left.

cards.front: Do we need proof of the crime?
cards.back: No. You need grounds for suspicion based on facts. Proving the crime is law enforcement's job.

cards.front: Wait a few weeks to see if the pattern continues?
cards.back: No. File promptly once suspicion is formed; file again if activity continues. Check your local rules for any deadlines.

cards.front: Compliance decided not to file after my escalation. Must I file myself?
cards.back: No. You met your duty by escalating internally; compliance documents its reasons. Escalate again if new facts appear.

cards.front: Is good-faith reporting risky for me?
cards.back: No. FATF standards require countries to protect reporting entities and staff from liability for reports made in good faith.

cards.title: Write a narrative the FIU can use
cards.body:
Answer **who, what, when, where, how and why**:
- **Who:** customer, related parties and counterparties, with identifiers
- **What, when, where:** amounts, dates, branches, channels
- **How:** the pattern, such as structured cash or rapid pass-through
- **Why suspicious:** how it departs from the profile
- **What you did:** CDD reviewed, explanation sought

Good: 'Between 2 and 23 March, 41 cash deposits of MYR 9,000–9,800 by 11 third parties at 7 branches; 90% sent onward within 48 hours to accounts in London. Profiled as a phone shop; owner could not name the source.' Avoid vague phrases and accusations of guilt.

cards.title: Real cases: the price of missed monitoring
cards.caption: Enforcement outcomes from four countries' regulators and courts, rounded. Each followed failures to monitor or to report.

items.label: Westpac, Australia, 2020
items.detail: Court-approved penalty for over 23 million breaches, including about 19.5 million unreported international transfers and weak monitoring for child exploitation risk.

items.label: HSBC, United States, 2012
items.detail: Deferred prosecution: weak monitoring let at least USD 881m of drug cartel proceeds pass through its US and Mexican operations.

items.label: NatWest, United Kingdom, 2021
items.detail: Criminal fine for failing to monitor a jeweller's deposits, about GBP 264m of them in cash.

items.label: CBA, Australia, 2018
items.detail: Over 53,000 late cash threshold reports from deposit machines, plus late or missing suspicious matter reports.

cards.title: Twenty minutes on instant payments
cards.body:
A retired teacher in Manchester falls for a fake investment app and sends GBP 12,000 to an account at our London unit. She reports it to her own bank within the hour.

Kwame looks at the receiving account: one of the app accounts linked to our trail, opened last month. Within **20 minutes** of her credit, most of the money left by instant payment to five other banks.

**What the bank prioritises:**
- immediate fraud recall and coordination with the other banks, because digital money moves in minutes
- escalating the receiving account as a possible **money mule**, with an STR if grounds exist
- near-real-time monitoring for new accounts with many unrelated incoming credits

Treating it as a mere complaint misses the laundering. Telling the account holder that the FIU will hear about it would be tipping off.

cards.title: Marco's 'quick fix'
cards.setting: Compliance floor, Dubai, Friday afternoon. Marco arrives holding a draft letter.

lines.text: Compliance filed an STR on Victor, right? So let's freeze his account and send him this letter: 'under review due to regulatory reporting'.
Two problems. An STR doesn't require a freeze; freezing is for sanctions matches or legal orders. And that letter tells him a report was made.
It doesn't even mention the FIU!
It doesn't need to. 'Regulatory reporting' says it all. Tipping off is an offence, and it can be committed by hinting.
Also, the access log shows someone in IT viewed Victor's account the day after Aisyah's escalation. He's Victor's brother-in-law.
Report that to compliance for an access review today. Information about escalations is strictly need-to-know.

cards.title: Tipping off and need-to-know
cards.body:
**Tipping off** means disclosing to a customer, or anyone not entitled to know, that a report has been or may be made, or that an investigation may follow. FATF requires countries to **prohibit** it, and in many it is a crime.

**Subtle ways it happens:**
- 'Compliance has flagged your account'
- A sudden freeze or closure with a hint about 'reporting'
- A relative on staff checking the account and warning the customer
- Accusatory questions after a decision to report

**After an STR,** the bank still decides on the relationship, such as a new loan request, on a risk basis, using the STR findings only within the need-to-know group and never citing them to the customer.

**Routine CDD questions are not tipping off.** Ask them as standard procedure, calmly.

cards.question: Two weeks after an STR on a trading customer, he asks for a higher overdraft limit. The credit team asks compliance what to do. What is the best approach?
options: Decline and tell him it is because of the report filed with the FIU
Approve as usual, because the STR is irrelevant to credit decisions
Assess the request on risk, using the STR findings within the need-to-know group, without disclosing anything
Ask the FIU to approve or reject the limit
cards.explanation: An STR is relevant to the bank's own risk decisions, so the request is assessed on risk with information shared only with those who need it. Citing the report is tipping off, ignoring it is imprudent, and the FIU does not make lending decisions.

cards.question: Which of these statements about the London app account that received 37 small transfers from strangers in two days, each moved out within minutes, is most accurate?
options: It looks like a new small business receiving sales receipts
It is a classic money mule pattern and should be escalated
No report is possible because each transfer is small
It should only be reported once a fraud victim complains
cards.explanation: A new account collecting many unrelated payments and emptying within minutes is the classic mule pattern for fraud proceeds. STRs have no minimum amount, and suspicion, not a victim complaint, is the trigger. Genuine businesses rarely empty accounts within minutes of every credit.

cards.title: Listening Post decoded
items: Monitoring compares activity with the CDD profile; every alert closure needs a written rationale, and backlogs mean late reports.
Know the patterns: structuring, mules, hawala settlement, agent abuse, under-invoiced exports and over-invoiced imports.
STRs have no threshold, cover attempts, need suspicion not proof, go promptly to the FIU via compliance, and are protected in good faith.
Cash threshold reports, where used (USD 10,000 in the US, AUD 10,000 in Australia), never replace an STR; accurate data lets the FIU link intelligence.
NatWest, Westpac, HSBC and CBA paid heavily for monitoring that missed what the profile and the counter staff were showing.
Escalating internally meets your duty; never advise customers how to avoid reports.
An STR doesn't require a freeze; hints, letters and staff relatives can all tip off, so keep it need-to-know.

cards.prompt: Imagine a regular customer asks you, 'Are you going to report me?' Write the exact words you would use to answer calmly without lying, without hinting at any report and without making him feel accused.

quiz.question: An analyst closes an alert with the note 'Customer is genuine, closed'. Why is this inadequate?
options: It does not record what was reviewed or why the activity fits the customer's profile
Alerts must always result in an STR, so closing an alert without filing is itself a breach of the reporting obligation
Only the compliance officer may close alerts
Closure notes must be written in two languages and countersigned by the branch manager before an alert can be closed
quiz.explanation: A closure rationale must show what was reviewed and why the activity is explained, so the decision can be checked later. Many alerts are legitimately closed without an STR, and closure authority depends on the institution's policy.

quiz.question: Which pattern is the clearest indicator of structuring?
options: A single large cash deposit, supported by a registered property sale deed and the buyer's transfer letter
Monthly salary credits from the same employer
Repeated cash deposits of similar amounts just below a threshold, spread across branches
An increase in deposits before a festive season, when retail sales rise
quiz.explanation: Structuring means splitting transactions to stay below thresholds, often across days or branches. A documented single deposit, regular salary and seasonal retail increases are consistent with legitimate activity.

quiz.question: Mr Malik, a customer at a money transfer business, receives remittances from twelve unrelated senders in four countries every month and withdraws each in cash the same day. He describes himself as a cook. What is the main concern?
options: That he should have opened a bank account instead
That his activity does not fit his profile and suggests he is collecting funds for others
That he may be evading income tax on his cooking income and should be reported to the tax authorities
That the money transfer business should file a cash threshold report with the FIU for each remittance he collects
quiz.explanation: Many unrelated senders, immediate cash withdrawal and a profile that does not fit point to the customer acting for others, a recognised hawala or mule indicator that needs escalation. Tax on his own income is not the issue here, and cash reports depend on cash thresholds, not on remittance receipt as such.

quiz.question: Which statement about suspicious transaction reports is correct?
options: STRs are only required for transactions above the cash reporting threshold
An STR can only be filed once the bank holds evidence sufficient to prove which predicate crime was committed
STRs must be filed only for completed transactions
An STR can be required for any amount, including an attempted transaction, once there are grounds for suspicion
quiz.explanation: STRs have no threshold, cover attempted transactions and require grounds for suspicion, not proof. Investigating and proving the crime is the role of law enforcement.

quiz.question: A bank's compliance officer forms a suspicion on a Monday but decides to wait a few weeks to see whether the customer's pattern continues before filing an STR. What is the problem?
options: None, because gathering more data first always produces a better and more useful STR for the FMU
The STR must be filed by the branch manager instead
STRs must be filed promptly once suspicion is formed; waiting breaches that duty
The STR should be replaced by a cash threshold report if the customer's pattern of deposits continues
quiz.explanation: Once suspicion is formed, reporting must be prompt. If further activity occurs, a further STR can be filed. Branch managers do not file STRs, and a cash threshold report never replaces an STR.

quiz.question: A new account opened via an app receives 37 small transfers from different people within two days, and almost all funds are moved to another bank within minutes of each credit. What is the most likely typology?
options: A legitimate small business that has started receiving sales receipts from new customers
A family collecting money for a wedding
A customer receiving salary from multiple employers
A money mule account used to collect and move fraud proceeds
quiz.explanation: A newly opened account with many incoming payments from unrelated people and immediate onward transfer is the classic mule pattern for fraud proceeds. Genuine businesses and families do not usually empty the account within minutes of each credit.

quiz.question: Under-invoicing of exports is most likely to be used to:
options: Keep part of the goods' true value abroad, often settled informally
Increase the export proceeds received into the exporter's home country so that it qualifies for incentives
Reduce the bank's trade finance fees
Comply with foreign customs valuation rules
quiz.explanation: Under-invoicing exports shows a lower value than the real one, so less money returns through banks and the balance can be kept or settled abroad, for example through hawala-style arrangements. It reduces, not increases, documented export proceeds.

quiz.question: Tariq, a teller, has escalated his concern about a customer to the branch's designated AML contact using the internal form. Compliance decides not to file an STR. What is Tariq's position?
options: He must now file an STR personally with the FIU, because he still has doubts
He has met his internal reporting duty; compliance should document why no STR was filed
He should inform the customer that the matter is closed
He must keep monitoring the customer's account personally every day
quiz.explanation: Staff meet their duty by escalating through the internal channel; the compliance officer makes and documents the filing decision. Telling the customer anything about the review risks tipping off, and personal monitoring is not his role. If new facts arise later, he can escalate again.

quiz.question: A customer asks a teller: 'What amount can I deposit in cash without the bank reporting it?' What is the correct approach?
options: Tell him the exact threshold so that he can plan his deposits, since the rules are public anyway
Refuse to serve him and close his account immediately
Not advise on avoiding reports, say standard procedures apply, and escalate if warranted
Tell him that all deposits are reported, even if this is not accurate
quiz.explanation: Staff must not help customers avoid reporting, and an interest in avoiding thresholds is a red flag worth escalating. Closing the account at once is disproportionate and may tip off, and giving false information is unprofessional.

quiz.question: After filing an STR, a bank immediately freezes the customer's account and sends him a letter saying it is 'under review due to regulatory reporting'. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, because banks must freeze all accounts subject to STRs
Nothing, because the letter does not name the FIU or say that an STR was filed
Only the freeze is wrong; the letter is fine
An STR does not itself require a freeze, and the letter risks tipping off
quiz.explanation: An STR does not by itself require a freeze; freezing applies, for example, to sanctions matches or legal orders. Referring to 'regulatory reporting' signals that a report has been made, risking tipping off, whether or not the FIU is named.

sessions.title: Targeted Financial Sanctions and the Compliance Programme
sessions.summary: In the vault, assets are locked down and the whole programme is tested. Learn how UN and national sanctions lists work, how to screen and handle matches, how to freeze and report without delay, and what an effective AML/CFT/CPF compliance programme needs from the board down.
objectives: Explain targeted financial sanctions for TF and PF and their UN and national sources
Screen customers and transactions effectively and resolve potential matches
Apply freezing and reporting obligations without delay and without prior notice
Recognise proliferation financing red flags in trade
Describe the governance, compliance officer, training and audit elements of a programme, and learn from real cases where programmes failed

cards.title: 9:40 pm: the list changes
cards.setting: The Vault: the sanctions desk, Dubai, late on a Thursday. Kwame is on call.

lines.text: Your phone buzzes after dinner. Kwame: 'List update just landed. You need to see this.'
A UN Security Council sanctions committee has added new names. Our rescreen flagged one: Anton Brandt, beneficiary of one of the London app accounts in our trail.
The passport number on the list entry matches our record digit for digit. Same date of birth, same nationality.
He also has a joint savings account with his wife at our Nairobi branch, and he owns 100 percent of a small transport company that banks there.
(joining the call) Then this is no longer about suspicion. A confirmed match means we freeze, without delay and without warning him. Tonight.
Welcome to the Vault, the final stage. Here we lock assets down and test whether the whole programme really works.

scenes.heading: Aimed at names, not countries
scenes.narration: Targeted financial sanctions hit specific designated people, groups and entities. They serve two goals: stopping terrorist financing, and stopping the financing of weapons of mass destruction.

scenes.heading: Source one: the UN
scenes.narration: UN Security Council committees designate names, for example under resolution 1267 for ISIL and Al-Qaida, and resolution 1718 for North Korea's weapons programmes. Every country must give these designations legal effect without delay, through its own laws.

scenes.heading: Source two: national lists
scenes.narration: Countries also designate under their own laws, as resolution 1373 requires: think of the UAE's Local Terrorist List, the EU and UK lists, or Pakistan's proscription schedules. And the US enforces its own OFAC lists, which reach any bank that clears US dollars.

scenes.heading: Two core duties
scenes.narration: Freeze the funds and assets of designated persons without delay and without prior notice. And never make funds or services available to them, directly or indirectly, unless the competent authority authorises it.

scenes.heading: Everyone, everything
scenes.narration: These duties apply to everyone in the country, not just banks. They cover assets owned or controlled jointly or indirectly, including companies the designated person owns or controls. In the US, OFAC treats companies owned fifty percent or more by blocked persons as blocked too.

scenes.heading: Not the same as an STR
scenes.narration: An STR needs suspicion and judgement. A freeze needs only a confirmed match. If the person is designated, you freeze. No suspicion required.

cards.title: From alert to freeze
cards.caption: Check reporting recipients, formats and deadlines with your national sanctions authority, for example OFAC in the US, OFSI in the UK or the Executive Office for Control and Non-Proliferation in the UAE.

items.label: Receive the list update
items.detail: Automated intake, including outside business hours.

items.label: Rescreen immediately
items.detail: Customers, beneficial owners, signatories and pending transactions.

items.label: Compare identifiers
items.detail: Passport or ID number, date of birth, nationality: true match, false positive or inconclusive.

items.label: Freeze without delay
items.detail: All accounts, joint holdings, lockers and controlled companies. No warning to the person.

items.label: Report as instructed
items.detail: Report the freeze and any attempted transactions; file an STR on related suspicious activity.

items.label: Keep it frozen
items.detail: Release only on delisting, a proven false match or competent-authority authorisation.

cards.title: Freeze it or not?
cards.prompt: It's 10:15 pm. For each item, decide: does the freeze obligation apply?

items.text: Anton Brandt's personal current account and app account
His joint savings account with his wife, who is not listed
The transport company he wholly owns and controls
Profit credited by the bank to his frozen account next month
A locker held in his name
Victor Lau's account, which has an STR but no designation
A namesake whose passport number and date of birth clearly differ from the list
An account of someone delisted, confirmed not on any other list or order

cards.question: A screening alert matches customer 'Mohammad Yousaf Rehmani' against list entry 'Muhammad Yusuf Rahmani'. The list entry shows a passport number and date of birth. What should the analyst do first?
options: Clear it, because every name is spelled differently
Freeze the account at once because the names sound alike
Compare the passport number and other identifiers with the customer's records
Phone the customer to ask whether he has been designated
cards.explanation: Transliteration differences like Mohammad/Muhammad and Rehmani/Rahmani are common, so spelling can neither clear nor confirm a match. Secondary identifiers decide. Freezing on similarity alone is premature, and calling the customer could warn a designated person.

cards.front: UN resolution 1267 regime
cards.back: UN sanctions on ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida, run by a Security Council committee: the core UN list for terrorist financing freezes.

cards.front: UN resolution 1373
cards.back: Requires countries to designate terrorists themselves: the basis for national lists such as the UAE's Local Terrorist List or Pakistan's proscription schedules.

cards.front: Without delay
cards.back: Freeze ideally within hours of designation, which needs automated list intake, immediate rescreening and clearly delegated authority.

cards.front: Without prior notice
cards.back: Never warn the designated person before freezing; they could move the assets.

cards.front: The designated person's wife claims half the joint account
cards.back: The account stays frozen. Refer her claim to compliance and the competent authority; the bank doesn't release funds itself.

cards.front: A frozen customer has just been delisted by the UN
cards.back: Confirm the delisting and that no other list, such as a national or US list, or legal order applies, then unfreeze promptly as officially instructed.

cards.front: Request for basic living expenses from frozen funds
cards.back: Only where the law allows and the competent authority has authorised it. Refer to compliance.

cards.title: Real case: BNP Paribas and the stripped payments
cards.body:
**What happened.** In 2014 BNP Paribas, France's largest bank, pleaded guilty in the US to processing thousands of US-dollar payments for parties in Sudan, Iran and Cuba in breach of US sanctions, mainly between 2004 and 2012. It agreed to pay about **USD 8.9bn**, and some of its US-dollar clearing was suspended for a year.

**How it was hidden, according to US authorities:** payments were routed through other banks and stripped of references to sanctioned parties so that US screening filters would not stop them, and warnings from compliance staff were not acted on.

**Lessons for every bank, not only US ones:**
- US sanctions can reach any bank that clears US dollars
- removing or disguising payment details to avoid screening is a serious breach
- when compliance raises an alarm, the business must not quietly overrule it

cards.title: Pressure at the Vault door
cards.setting: Friday morning, Dubai. The overnight work is under review.

lines.text: The transport company has been a client of mine for years. Can't we wait until Monday and let me call him politely first? It's only courtesy.
No. Freezing is immediate and without prior notice. A polite call is still a warning, and a weekend is plenty of time to empty an account.
There's another problem. The list update produced 400 potential matches overnight. A junior analyst wants to bulk-clear every alert with a common first name.
And on the trade side: a brand-new Singapore-registered firm wants an LC for precision CNC machine tools for a buyer in a third country. They call end-use details 'confidential'.
Three pressure tests in one morning. This is exactly where programmes fail. Let's handle them one at a time.

cards.title: 400 alerts and a deadline
cards.situation: After the list update, the screening queue shows 400 potential matches. Most involve very common names such as Mohammed, Ali, Wang or Garcia. The team is three people short, Marco is complaining that customers' transfers are held, and the junior analyst proposes bulk-clearing every alert where only a common first name matched. You're the duty lead. What do you decide?

choices.text: Approve the bulk clearance. Common names are almost always false positives.
choices.outcome: Designated persons often have common names. One cleared alert was a true match; his transfer left the bank the same afternoon. That is a missed freeze, a breach of TFS obligations and a likely enforcement case.

choices.text: Refuse bulk clearance; triage by risk, check identifiers on every alert, call in extra analysts, and log a request to tune the matching rules.
choices.outcome: The queue takes longer, but every clearance is backed by identifiers on file. One genuine match is found and frozen. The tuning request later cuts false positives without loosening matching. The right call.

choices.text: Loosen the fuzzy-matching settings so fewer alerts appear in future.
choices.outcome: It fixes tomorrow's workload by making the system blind. Too-strict matching lets true matches slip through. Tuning must be tested so true positives aren't lost, and today's 400 still need checking.

choices.text: Clear only alerts where the customer has banked with you for over five years.
choices.outcome: Better than clearing on names alone, but tenure isn't an identifier. A long-standing customer can be newly designated, exactly as tonight. Only identifier checks can clear an alert.

cards.title: Proliferation financing hides in trade
cards.body:
PF rarely looks like a weapons deal. It looks like ordinary industrial trade.

**The international frame:** UN Security Council resolution 1540 (2004) requires every country to control goods that could help build weapons of mass destruction, and resolutions such as 1718 (2006) on North Korea impose targeted financial sanctions. Countries run export controls, for example the EU dual-use regulation, the US Export Administration Regulations, Singapore's Strategic Goods (Control) Act and Pakistan's Export Control Act 2004.

**Red flags:**
- **Dual-use goods:** machine tools, vacuum pumps, special metals, certain chemicals and electronics
- **End user:** vague, changing or undisclosed, or a trader with no industrial use
- **Route and parties:** pointless transshipment, new intermediaries, shared addresses, unrelated payers

**Response:** escalate to compliance for checks on goods, parties, vessels and route. Goods needn't be on a control list to be relevant.

cards.question: Which transaction is the strongest proliferation financing red flag?
options: A long-standing rice exporter shipping basmati to a Gulf supermarket chain under a confirmed LC
A new trading firm financing precision CNC machine tools for a third-country buyer, refusing end-use details
A pharmaceutical distributor buying medicines from a local manufacturer
An edible oil importer paying a known supplier by letter of credit
cards.explanation: Machine tools can be dual-use, and a new intermediary refusing end-use information is a classic PF warning sign that needs escalation. The other transactions describe ordinary trade by established businesses with no PF-specific concerns.

cards.title: The compliance programme engine
cards.caption: A programme works only when each part feeds the next, round and round.

items.label: Board sets direction
items.detail: Approves policy and risk appetite; oversees through meaningful MIS.

items.label: Management resources it
items.detail: Staff, systems, data; ML/TF/PF risk built into business decisions.

items.label: First line applies controls
items.detail: Branches and business units own the risk day to day.

items.label: Compliance monitors and challenges
items.detail: Independent officer with authority, resources and direct board access.

items.label: Audit tests in practice
items.detail: Samples real files, alerts, STRs and screening results.

items.label: Findings flow back up
items.detail: Tracked remediation reported to the board.

cards.title: Who owns what?
cards.prompt: Match each player to their AML/CFT/CPF responsibility.

pairs.right: Approve the policy and risk appetite and oversee the programme through regular, meaningful reports
Independent, with real authority, resources and direct board access; decides on STRs
First line: own the risk and apply CDD, screening and escalation every day
Third line: independently test whether controls work by sampling real files and alerts
Screen staff integrity and ensure role-based training is completed and recorded

cards.title: What your board should see
cards.caption: Illustrative MIS from the bank's quarterly AML report. 'STRs filed: 2' alone tells a board nothing.

items.label: High-risk customers
items.detail: With EDD reviews overdue tracked separately.

items.label: Alerts older than 30 days
items.detail: Backlogs mean late STRs.

items.label: List update to rescreen
items.detail: Too slow for 'without delay'; the target is hours.

items.label: Trade staff trained on TBML/PF
items.detail: Role-based training completion.

items.label: Open audit and inspection findings
items.detail: With owners and deadlines.

cards.title: When the programme fails
cards.body:
**Independent testing** must check that controls work in practice: was CDD complete, were alerts closed with sound reasons, were STRs prompt, were list updates applied without delay? An audit that only checks policies exist tells you nothing about effectiveness. Compliance can't audit its own work.

**For institutions:** monetary penalties, which supervisors worldwide impose and often publish, even without proof that a specific crime's proceeds passed through; business restrictions such as growth caps or suspended services; remediation; lost correspondents.

**For individuals:** disciplinary action, regulatory penalties and, for offences such as tipping off or knowingly assisting laundering, criminal liability. Not just the compliance officer: in real cases, chief executives and branch staff have faced charges.

Staff who escalate in good faith are protected.

cards.title: Real case: Binance and compliance as an afterthought
cards.body:
**What happened.** In November 2023 Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, pleaded guilty in the US to failing to maintain an effective AML programme, operating an unlicensed money transmitting business and breaching US sanctions. It agreed to pay about **USD 4.3bn**. Its founder and chief executive also pleaded guilty to an AML programme failure and stepped down.

**What US authorities found:**
- growth came first: for years many users could trade without full identity checks
- it did not report more than **100,000** suspicious transactions, including some linked to terrorist groups and ransomware
- it processed trades between US users and users in sanctioned countries such as Iran

**Lesson:** compliance culture is set at the top. A programme that leaders treat as optional fails, however advanced the technology.

cards.question: The bank's compliance officer reports to the head of retail, whose bonus depends on account growth, and has no direct access to the board. Several high-risk accounts were opened over compliance's objections. What is the most important fix?
options: Give the compliance officer an independent reporting line, direct board access, real authority and resources
Send the compliance officer on extra AML training
Ask compliance to file more STRs to show the board it is active
Move compliance under internal audit
cards.explanation: The compliance officer needs independence and board access to resist business pressure. Training doesn't fix a conflict of interest, extra STRs would be defensive filing, and putting compliance under audit would compromise audit's independence as the third line.

cards.title: Training that changes behaviour
cards.body: A 20-minute generic e-learning module for everyone rarely satisfies inspectors. Make it **role-based**: tellers practise structuring and mule cases, trade staff study TBML and dual-use goods, relationship managers rehearse PEP and source-of-wealth conversations, and board members learn oversight. Use local typologies, test understanding, keep records, and update when rules or risks change.

cards.title: The final boss: the boardroom
cards.setting: Board Risk Committee, Dubai head office. Everyone you've met is in the room or on screen.

lines.text: The floor is yours. Take the board through the trail, from Kuala Lumpur to the Vault.
It started at my counter in KL: strangers depositing structured cash for Victor Lau at seven branches. Placement, through a mule.
Then London app accounts opened with other people's identities, layering the money into Quillon Trading.
Quillon's sister firm paid for under-invoiced fabric through my Singapore desk, with the balance settled abroad. Trade-based laundering.
A USD 250,000 'gift' from offshore reached Pieter Vos, close associate of a foreign PEP. Integration. And one account beneficiary turned out to be on a UN sanctions list.
I'll admit it: two of my 'growth' ideas would have made this worse. What does the board need to decide?
That is your next decision, and your last test before the final exam.

cards.title: Presenting to the board
cards.situation: You have ten minutes with the Board Risk Committee. One director interrupts: 'Before you start, give us the full names of everyone we filed STRs on. We need to know who we're dealing with.' You need to answer him and then set out what the board must decide.

choices.text: Read out the names. Directors are entitled to everything.
choices.outcome: STR subjects are strictly need-to-know. Sharing names widely breaches confidentiality and multiplies tipping-off risk. The compliance officer has to step in, and the minutes record the breach.

choices.text: Politely explain STR subjects stay within the need-to-know group, then present what happened, the freezes and reports made, the control gaps found, and the decisions needed.
choices.outcome: The chair backs you. You show the trail, the gaps (mule accounts passed ID checks without profile questions, no trade price comparison, slow list rescreening) and ask the board to set risk appetite for app onboarding and fund price analytics and automated screening. The board approves.

choices.text: Skip the case and show only the number of STRs filed this year.
choices.outcome: No names leak, but the board learns nothing about whether controls work. 'STRs filed' alone is exactly the thin MIS inspectors criticise.

cards.title: Vault secured
items: TFS come from UN designations (such as the 1267 and 1718 regimes) and national lists required by resolution 1373; US OFAC lists reach anyone clearing US dollars.
A confirmed match means freeze without delay and without notice; no suspicion is needed, unlike an STR.
Freezes cover joint, indirect and controlled assets, including wholly owned companies; profit credited stays frozen.
Resolve matches with identifiers; never bulk-clear common names; unfreeze only on confirmed delisting or official instruction.
PF hides in trade: dual-use goods, undisclosed end users, transshipment and new intermediaries.
Boards set appetite and oversee with real MIS; compliance must be independent; audit must sample real files. BNP Paribas and Binance show failures hit institutions and leaders.

cards.prompt: If a new name were added to a sanctions or proscription list at 9 pm tonight, how quickly would your institution find out, rescreen its customers and freeze a match? Where exactly could that chain break, and who would you tell?

quiz.question: What distinguishes a targeted financial sanctions freeze from an STR?
options: A freeze requires a suspicion of terrorism, while an STR requires a confirmed match to a sanctions list
A freeze follows a confirmed match to a designation list without needing suspicion, while an STR depends on suspicion
Both depend on the institution's judgement about whether a crime occurred
A freeze is only applied after the FIU approves the STR
quiz.explanation: TFS obligations arise from designation itself: if a customer is a confirmed match, assets must be frozen without delay. STRs require grounds for suspicion and judgement. The FIU does not approve freezes.

quiz.question: Which UN Security Council resolution requires countries to designate terrorists under their own laws, forming the basis of national lists such as the UAE's Local Terrorist List?
options: Resolution 1373
Resolution 1267
Resolution 1718
Resolution 1540
quiz.explanation: Resolution 1373 requires countries to freeze assets of terrorists they designate themselves, which underpins national lists. Resolution 1267 created the UN list now covering ISIL and Al-Qaida, 1718 imposes sanctions on North Korea, and 1540 requires controls on WMD-related goods.

quiz.question: A bank freezes the personal account of a designated person but continues to process payments for a company he wholly owns and controls. What is the problem?
options: There is no problem, because the company is a separate legal person with its own account and directors
The bank should have closed the company account instead of freezing the personal account
Assets he owns or controls indirectly, such as his company's, must also be frozen
The bank only needs to file a CTR for the company's payments
quiz.explanation: TFS cover funds owned or controlled, directly or indirectly, by designated persons, which includes companies they own or control. Continuing to serve the company can make funds available to the designated person. Separate legal personality does not shield the assets.

quiz.question: Hassan's screening alert shows a customer named 'Muhammad Abdur Rahman' against a list entry for 'Mohammad Abdul Rehman'. The list entry includes a passport number. What should he do first?
options: Clear the alert, because the spellings of both the first name and the family name differ from the list
Freeze the account immediately because the names are similar
Ask the customer to confirm whether he has ever been designated
Compare the passport number and other identifiers on the list with the customer's records
quiz.explanation: Transliteration differences are common, so spelling alone cannot clear or confirm a match. Secondary identifiers such as the passport number decide whether it is a true match. Freezing on similarity alone is premature, and asking the customer is inappropriate.

quiz.question: A designated person's frozen account receives a profit payment from the bank's own deposit product. What should happen to it?
options: It should be paid out in cash to the account holder
It may be credited, but it remains frozen
It should be returned to the bank as income
It should be transferred to the FIU
quiz.explanation: Under the TFS framework, additions such as interest or profit due on frozen accounts can be credited but remain frozen. Paying them out would make funds available to the designated person, and the FIU does not hold frozen funds.

quiz.question: Which situation is the strongest proliferation financing red flag?
options: A garment exporter shipping finished goods to an established European buyer under a confirmed letter of credit
An importer of edible oil paying by letter of credit
A pharmaceutical distributor buying medicines from a local manufacturer
A new trading firm buying machine tools for an undisclosed end user via a transshipment hub
quiz.explanation: Dual-use goods, an undisclosed end user, a trading firm with no industrial use and indirect routing together are typical PF indicators. The other transactions describe ordinary trade with no PF-specific concerns.

quiz.question: Which arrangement best supports freezing 'without delay'?
options: Monthly batch screening of the customer base against updated lists
Freezing only after the branch manager has met the customer
Automated receipt of list updates, immediate rescreening and clearly delegated authority to freeze
Waiting for the regulator to confirm each potential match in writing before acting
quiz.explanation: Freezing without delay requires fast list ingestion, immediate rescreening and clear authority to act. Monthly batches and waiting for confirmation letters create delays, and meeting the customer risks prior notice.

quiz.question: Which is the board's most important AML/CFT/CPF responsibility?
options: Approving the policy and risk appetite, and overseeing the programme through regular, meaningful reporting
Personally reviewing every STR before it is filed, to ensure the bank's reputation is protected
Screening all new customers against sanctions lists
Deciding which alerts should be closed
quiz.explanation: The board sets direction and oversees effectiveness. Reviewing individual STRs would undermine confidentiality and the compliance officer's role, and screening and alert handling are operational tasks for the first and second lines.

quiz.question: An internal audit of AML/CFT reviews only whether policies exist and are approved, without sampling any customer files or alerts. What is the main weakness?
options: Internal audit should never review AML/CFT
It does not test whether controls work in practice, so effectiveness is unknown
Audit should only sample STRs, not policies
The review should have been carried out by the compliance officer, who knows the controls best
quiz.explanation: Independent testing must check effectiveness by sampling real files, alerts, STRs and screening results, not just the existence of documents. Compliance cannot independently audit its own work, and audit should cover policies as well as practice.

quiz.question: In 2023 a global cryptocurrency exchange and its chief executive both pleaded guilty in the US over AML failures. Which general statement about the consequences of AML/CFT failures is accurate?
options: Institutions can be penalised, and individuals, including senior leaders, can face disciplinary, regulatory or even criminal consequences
Only institutions can be penalised; individual staff and leaders are never personally liable
Penalties can only be imposed if it is proven that a specific crime's proceeds passed through the institution
Penalties are always kept confidential and never published
quiz.explanation: Supervisors penalise institutions for control failures even without proof that a specific crime passed through, and individuals can face disciplinary, regulatory and criminal consequences, as Binance's founder did in 2023. Supervisors in many countries publish enforcement actions.

bank.question: A customs official takes bribes in cash. He (1) deposits the cash into his wife's account in small amounts, (2) transfers it among three relatives' accounts and a cousin's 'construction' firm, and (3) later receives a 'consultancy fee' from that firm to buy a house. Which step is the layering stage?
options: Step 1, because the cash is split into small amounts to avoid attention
Step 3, because receiving a consultancy fee from the firm creates a false explanation for where the funds came from
Step 2, because moving funds among relatives and a firm breaks the link to the bribes
None, because the funds never left the country
bank.explanation: Layering is the movement of funds through successive transactions to obscure their origin, which is what the transfers among relatives and the firm do. Step 1 is placement and step 3, giving the money a legitimate-looking explanation for a purchase, is integration. Laundering does not require a foreign leg.

bank.question: A salaried engineer in London sends GBP 150 every month to a 'welfare' collector. Months later it emerges that the collector raises funds for a banned terrorist group operating under a new name. The engineer's salary is fully legitimate. How should this be analysed?
options: It may be TF: what matters is the funds' purpose and destination, not their lawful source
It cannot be terrorist financing because the salary is fully legitimate, taxed income
It is money laundering, because the funds were moved through a bank account
It is only a regulatory breach by the bank for weak monitoring, not a possible offence by the engineer
bank.explanation: TF can use clean money; what matters is that funds are provided or collected for terrorist purposes or organisations, and knowledge and intent are for investigators to establish. Laundering concerns disguising criminal proceeds, which is not the issue here. The bank's controls are a separate question.

bank.question: A colleague argues that the UAE's 2022 grey-listing meant UAE banks were legally barred from dealing with foreign banks. Which statement best corrects him?
options: He is right: grey-listing triggers a ban on correspondent relationships with the listed country under the FATF Recommendations
He is right only for banks with foreign branches
Grey-listing only affects government borrowing and has no effect on banks
No legal ban followed, but foreign banks applied more scrutiny, raising costs and correspondent pressure
bank.explanation: Jurisdictions under increased monitoring are not subject to a legal ban; FATF does not call for countermeasures against them. In practice, foreign banks factor the listing into their risk assessments, increasing checks and costs. Countermeasures are associated with the call-for-action list.

bank.question: A country's laws are found to be largely compliant with the FATF Recommendations, but very few STRs result in investigations and almost no criminal proceeds are confiscated. How would assessors most likely view this?
options: As fully satisfactory, because technical compliance is what FATF mainly assesses
As an effectiveness gap: sound laws are not producing results
As a technical compliance failure that can only be fixed by enacting new legislation
As irrelevant, because confiscation is assessed only for grey-listed countries
bank.explanation: Effectiveness is assessed separately from technical compliance. Good laws without investigations or confiscation show the system is not working, lowering effectiveness ratings. New laws would not fix a problem of implementation, and all countries are assessed on both dimensions.

bank.question: Which pairing of country and AML/CFT framework is correct?
options: United Kingdom: the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 alongside the Money Laundering Regulations 2017
United Arab Emirates: suspicious transaction reports are filed with FinCEN
Singapore: STRO, the FIU, is also the supervisor that inspects banks
United States: suspicious activity reports are filed with the National Crime Agency
bank.explanation: The UK's main AML laws are POCA 2002 and the Money Laundering Regulations 2017. UAE reporting entities file with the UAE FIU, not FinCEN; in Singapore STRO receives reports while MAS supervises; and US SARs go to FinCEN, while the National Crime Agency houses the UK FIU.

bank.question: An insurance company in Singapore identifies suspicious early surrender of large single-premium policies funded by third parties. Which describes the correct reporting and supervisory relationship?
options: The insurer files an STR with MAS, which forwards it to the police
The insurer files an STR with STRO, the FIU; MAS supervises its AML/CFT compliance
The insurer reports to STRO, which is also its AML/CFT supervisor
The insurer reports only to its regional FATF-style body
bank.explanation: Reporting entities file STRs with the national FIU, which in Singapore is STRO. MAS is the AML/CFT supervisor for financial institutions, including insurers. The FIU is not the supervisor, and regional bodies assess countries rather than receive reports.

bank.question: FATF publicly identifies two groups of jurisdictions. Which statement correctly contrasts them?
options: Grey-listed jurisdictions face mandatory countermeasures from all FATF members, while black-listed jurisdictions face only enhanced monitoring of their action plans
Both lists lead to automatic UN Security Council sanctions on the listed countries
Jurisdictions under increased monitoring are those without any AML law; call-for-action jurisdictions have weak supervision only
Grey-listed jurisdictions work through action plans; for call-for-action jurisdictions FATF calls for EDD and, at worst, countermeasures
bank.explanation: Grey-listed jurisdictions have committed to action plans to fix deficiencies. For call-for-action (black list) jurisdictions, FATF calls on members to apply enhanced due diligence and, in the most serious cases, countermeasures. FATF listing does not itself create UN sanctions.

bank.question: A grey-listed country wants to be removed from FATF's list of jurisdictions under increased monitoring. What does that require, as Pakistan and the UAE both showed?
options: Substantially completing its agreed action plan, confirmed by an on-site visit
Paying a fee to the FATF secretariat and its regional body
Passing a single new AML law, after which removal is automatic
Obtaining a resolution of the UN Security Council
bank.explanation: Pakistan (removed October 2022) and the UAE (removed February 2024) were both removed after FATF judged their action plans substantially complete and an on-site visit confirmed implementation. Removal is not bought, not automatic on new legislation and not a UN Security Council decision.

bank.question: A trader hides drug proceeds as 'profit' from his rice business and himself moves the funds through several company accounts. His lawyer claims he cannot be charged with laundering because he committed the underlying crime himself. In the FATF framework, which is the best response?
options: The lawyer is right: laundering can only be committed by a third party
The lawyer is right if the drug offence is prosecuted first, because laundering charges can only follow a conviction
Laundering is a separate offence, and it can be committed by the same person who committed the underlying predicate offence
Laundering only applies if the proceeds were moved abroad
bank.explanation: Laundering is distinct from the predicate offence, and the standards expect self-laundering to be criminalised. A person can face charges for both the drug offence and laundering. Laundering does not require a cross-border element or a third party.

bank.question: During a mutual evaluation, assessors interview a bank's branch staff in a provincial town. Why would assessors want to speak to front-line staff rather than only to head office compliance?
options: Because FATF requires every bank branch to have its own designated compliance officer who must be interviewed
Because effectiveness depends on whether staff actually apply CDD and escalation day to day
Because branch staff file STRs directly with the FIU
Because assessors are only allowed to visit branches outside major cities
bank.explanation: Effectiveness assessment looks at whether obligations work in practice, which depends on front-line understanding and behaviour. Branch staff escalate internally rather than filing STRs themselves, and there is no requirement for a compliance officer in every branch.

bank.question: A bank rates its outward remittance business as high inherent risk. Its controls are well designed, but testing shows that 30 percent of high-risk remittance alerts were closed without review. How should residual risk be assessed?
options: Low, because the controls are well designed
Inherent risk should be reduced to medium to reflect the well-designed controls
Residual risk cannot be assessed until the supervisor inspects
High, because it is control effectiveness, not design, that reduces risk
bank.explanation: Residual risk depends on how well controls work in practice. Evidence of ineffective alert handling means risk is not being reduced as designed. Inherent risk does not change because of controls, and institutions must assess their own risk without waiting for an inspection.

bank.question: A bank is about to open branches in border regions that its country's national risk assessment identifies as exposed to cross-border smuggling. Which response best reflects the risk-based approach?
options: Refuse to open the branches, because geographic risk cannot be managed
Update the risk assessment and calibrate controls for those branches, without refusing customers from the area
Open the branches under the same controls used elsewhere, because geographic risk only concerns foreign countries and not domestic regions
Rate every customer from those districts as high risk regardless of profile
bank.explanation: The RBA calls for understanding the elevated risk and calibrating controls accordingly, not blanket refusal or blanket high-risk ratings, which amount to de-risking. Domestic geographic risk identified in the national assessment is relevant and should not be ignored.

bank.question: A customer-risk model gives 'customer type', 'product', 'geography' and 'channel' equal weight and averages them. A domestic NPO operating in an area of TF concern, using only a basic current account at a local branch, therefore scores 'low'. What is the main flaw?
options: Averaging lets low factors dilute a serious one; a high-risk factor should be able to drive the rating
The model should never include channel risk
NPOs should be excluded from risk models
The score is correct, because three of the four factors are genuinely low and the model must be applied consistently
bank.explanation: Simple averaging can hide serious risk. Good models allow certain factors, such as TF exposure, PEP status or sanctions links, to drive the rating or trigger a minimum rating. Channel risk is a valid factor, and NPOs must be risk-rated like other customers.

bank.question: Which statement about the enterprise-wide risk assessment is most accurate?
options: It is required only for banks, not for money service businesses, insurers or DNFBPs
It replaces the need to risk-rate individual customers
It must cover ML, TF and PF, be approved at senior level and be updated on material change
It should be completed once at licensing and then kept unchanged so that results remain comparable year to year
bank.explanation: Institutional risk assessments must cover ML, TF and PF, be documented, approved and kept current, including after material changes. Reporting entities beyond banks must assess risk too. Customer-level ratings are still needed to apply proportionate CDD.

bank.question: A payment fintech wants to raise wallet limits for customers onboarded through agents, without stronger verification, to grow volumes before year end. The compliance head objects. Which argument is strongest under the RBA?
options: Higher limits raise mule risk, so they should rise only with stronger verification and monitoring
Higher limits are always prohibited for wallets
Only the FIU can approve changes to wallet limits
Agent-onboarded customers must always be rated high risk regardless of controls, so higher limits would breach policy
bank.explanation: The RBA links risk-increasing changes to matching controls. Higher limits for weakly verified, agent-onboarded wallets increase mule and fraud exposure. Tiered limits are allowed within regulatory rules, the FIU does not approve product limits, and blanket high ratings would ignore controls.

bank.question: A bank's analysis shows that 80 percent of its STRs relate to accounts opened through one digital channel, while the enterprise risk assessment rates that channel as low risk and monitoring rules for it were never updated. What should happen?
options: Nothing until the next scheduled annual update
The STRs should first be reviewed for defensive filing, because the channel has been rated low risk
The channel should be closed immediately
The channel's risk rating and controls should be reassessed in light of the evidence
bank.explanation: Internal data such as STR concentrations is a key input, and a significant mismatch is a trigger to revisit the assessment and controls; TD Bank shows the cost of monitoring that is not updated as risks change. Waiting ignores evidence, assuming defensive filing reverses the logic, and immediate closure is premature before analysis.

bank.question: A wealthy client of a bank's priority banking unit is rated high risk. The unit head proposes reducing EDD reviews to once every three years 'to improve client experience'. Which response is correct?
options: Approve, provided the client signs an annual self-declaration confirming that his circumstances have not changed
Refuse: review frequency follows the risk rating, and client convenience is not a risk reason
Approve, because review frequency is a commercial decision
Downgrade the client to medium so that the longer cycle applies
bank.explanation: Review frequency is tied to risk under policy, and changes need risk-based justification. A self-declaration does not replace EDD, and downgrading to reach a preferred review cycle is a classic improper override.

bank.question: Under the risk-based approach, which obligation applies regardless of a customer's low risk rating?
options: Obtaining source of wealth evidence, because every customer's total net worth must be understood under the RBA
Senior management approval at onboarding
Sanctions and proscription screening, and reporting suspicion if it arises
Annual site visits
bank.explanation: Low risk can justify lighter CDD, but sanctions screening and reporting suspicion are never switched off. Source of wealth, senior management approval and site visits are enhanced measures that apply to higher-risk relationships.

bank.question: A bank exits all accounts of licensed money service businesses after a single one is fined, even those with strong controls and clean histories. A year later, the bank notices a rise in unexplained cash and transfers linked to informal money transfer in its retail accounts. What best explains this?
options: Licensed money service businesses are unregulated, so exiting them made no difference
The FIU stopped receiving STRs from money service businesses
The rise is unrelated, because informal transfer never uses bank accounts
Blanket de-risking pushed legitimate flows into informal channels that now pass unseen through retail accounts
bank.explanation: FATF warns that de-risking can drive activity into less transparent channels. Licensed money service businesses are supervised, and informal transfer frequently uses ordinary accounts to settle balances. The exit removed visibility without managing the underlying risk.

bank.question: Which situation best justifies a documented downward override of a model-generated 'high' rating?
options: A state-owned utility whose large volumes are normal for its role, with transparent ownership and no adverse information
A jeweller who complains that EDD questions are intrusive
A PEP whose relationship manager has known him and his family personally for more than twenty years without issue
A customer who promises to reduce cash deposits next year
bank.explanation: An override is justified when the model misreads genuine risk, such as volumes that are normal for a state-owned utility with transparent ownership, and the reasoning is documented and approved. Complaints, personal familiarity and promises are not risk-based reasons.

bank.question: A private limited company applies for an account. Its shareholders are Ms Sara (20 percent), Mr Omar (20 percent) and an offshore company (60 percent) wholly owned by Mr Khalid, a businessman who also has the right to appoint all of the applicant's directors. Ms Sara and Mr Omar are unrelated to him and to each other. Assuming a 25 percent threshold applies, who is the beneficial owner?
options: Ms Sara and Mr Omar, because they are the only individuals holding shares directly
Mr Khalid, who owns 60 percent through the offshore company and controls board appointments
The offshore company, because it holds the majority of the shares
Nobody, because no individual holds 25 percent or more of the applicant's shares directly in their own name
bank.explanation: Ownership must be traced through intermediate companies to natural persons: Mr Khalid ultimately owns 60 percent and also controls the board, so he is the beneficial owner. Ms Sara and Mr Omar are below the threshold and have no stated control, though they are still identified as shareholders. A company can never be a beneficial owner.

bank.question: A sole trader running an electronics shop presents a passport that passes electronic verification, a tax registration certificate and a shop lease. His expected turnover is USD 500,000 a month, far above similar shops. What is the best CDD approach?
options: Accept the documents, since they are valid and verified, and set the expected turnover at the level the customer declared
Refuse the account, because sole traders are not permitted to have turnover above that of comparable shops in the area
Verify the business itself, such as by site visit and sales evidence, before agreeing a profile
Open the account and file a cash transaction report on the first deposit
bank.explanation: Documents prove existence on paper; an implausible turnover requires verifying the business and understanding the source of funds before setting the profile. Accepting the declared figure would make later monitoring meaningless, refusing outright is not risk-based, and a cash report is unrelated to onboarding judgement.

bank.question: A customer wants to open an account with an expired passport, saying he has applied for renewal and showing the receipt. What is the best approach for staff?
options: Open the account normally, since the passport number usually stays on file and a renewal is under way
Ask the customer to open the account in a relative's name until renewal
Refuse service permanently
Follow the bank's current procedure and the regulator's rules on expired identity documents
bank.explanation: Expired identity documents are covered by specific regulatory instructions and institutional procedures, and staff must follow them rather than improvise. Opening normally ignores the rules, using a relative's name creates a false account holder, and permanent refusal is disproportionate.

bank.question: Which customer most clearly requires enhanced due diligence under the FATF standards, regardless of the institution's own risk scoring?
options: A foreign PEP, such as a serving minister of another country, opening a personal account with a bank in Singapore
A local software house receiving payments from overseas clients
A domestic PEP whose relationship has been assessed as standard risk after the bank's review of his profile
A salaried employee of a multinational company in Toronto
bank.explanation: FATF requires enhanced measures for foreign PEPs in all cases. For domestic PEPs, enhanced measures apply when the relationship is assessed as higher risk, unless local regulations require more. The software house and the employee require EDD only if risk factors justify it.

bank.question: A foreign PEP's adult son opens an account and receives USD 250,000 from his father described as a 'gift' for buying a house. What is the most important EDD question?
options: Whether the son has a valid email address for statements
Whether the house is in a gated community
How the father built the wealth used for the gift, and whether it fits his known income
Whether the son already holds another bank account where he could have received the gift instead
bank.explanation: Family members of PEPs are treated as PEPs, and a large gift from the PEP makes the father's source of wealth central to judging corruption risk. The other questions do not address whether the funds could be proceeds of corruption.

bank.question: An NPO running flood relief in a remote region asks to receive large foreign donations. Its trustees screen clean, but the bank cannot find out which local partners actually distribute aid. What is the most proportionate response?
options: Ask about implementing partners and the use of funds, monitor closely, and then decide on accepting the foreign inflows
Close the account, because NPOs receiving large foreign donations fall outside any reasonable risk appetite
Accept the inflows without further questions, because humanitarian work is exempt from CDD
Accept the inflows but cap each donation at a small amount
bank.explanation: FATF expects targeted, risk-based measures for NPOs: understanding how and through whom funds are used, with enhanced monitoring where needed. Blanket exits harm legitimate charities, humanitarian work is not exempt, and an arbitrary cap does not address the missing information.

bank.question: A foreign respondent bank asks a bank in London to open a USD correspondent account. The respondent says several smaller banks in its region will also use the account to make payments. What is the key additional risk and response?
options: There is no added risk, because the respondent bank is licensed and supervised in its home country, which covers its users
Nested use: understand which banks will use the account and their controls, and restrict if needed
The only issue is currency risk, which treasury should manage
The London bank should file a cash transaction report on every payment through the account
bank.explanation: Nested relationships let other banks access the correspondent indirectly, so the correspondent bank must understand who they are and assess their controls, and may limit or decline the arrangement.
